articles.title: Record non-DSE admissions to Hong Kong’s universities spark calls for quotas
articles.summary: Hong Kong’s public universities admitted a record number of students applying outside the local Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) exam system, with non-DSE admissions rising by 63 per cent over seven years to nearly 30 per cent of the 15,000 government-funded undergraduate places. Concurrently, DSE student admissions declined by 7 per cent, reducing their share of those places from 82 per cent to 72 per cent.
articles.insight:
Hong Kong’s sharp rise in non-DSE admissions—especially from mainland China—may reflect shifting preferences among high-achieving Chinese students toward alternative pathways, though it remains unclear whether this signals broader regional demand shifts or is specific to Hong Kong’s policy and capacity constraints.  
Admissions teams should monitor mainland Chinese student application trends to Hong Kong versus traditional Anglophone destinations, as well as any policy adjustments in Hong Kong’s visa or scholarship frameworks that could influence cross-border mobility decisions.

articles.title: Taiwan’s international enrolment up by 17% in 2025/26
articles.summary: Taiwan’s international student enrolment reached 140,420 in the 2025/26 academic year, a 17% increase from the previous year and a new all-time high. Of these students, approximately 90,000 are enrolled in degree programmes, while the remainder consist of exchange students, Mandarin-language learners, and students from China and Hong Kong; the government’s target is 320,000 international students.
articles.insight:
Taiwan’s 17% international enrolment rise—driven partly by students from China and Hong Kong—may reflect shifting regional preferences, though it’s unclear whether this signals broader demand diversification or temporary policy-driven flows amid evolving cross-strait dynamics and global visa uncertainties.  
Admissions teams should monitor enrolment trends among Chinese and Hong Kong students in Taiwan versus traditional Anglophone destinations, as well as any concurrent changes in mainland China’s outbound study guidance, scholarship policies, or perceptions of academic quality and post-study opportunities.

articles.title: Jovens negros 'furam bolha' e conquistam bolsa para graduação no exterior
articles.summary: Three Black students have secured scholarships for undergraduate studies abroad. The announcement was published on August 23, 2026, at 3:00 PM.
articles.insight:
This news hints at growing aspiration among Black students in Latin America for undergraduate study abroad, potentially reflecting broader shifts in educational mobility—though it remains unclear whether this signals a sustained trend or isolated success amid persistent structural barriers.  
Admissions teams should track scholarship program uptake and alumni outcomes from similar cohorts, while reviewing outreach materials for cultural resonance and inclusivity, particularly in underrepresented communities across Latin America.

articles.title: Canada’s language training sector in “state of crisis” after further enrolment declines in 2025
articles.summary: Languages Canada’s 2025 Annual Survey Report states that the country’s language training sector is in a “state of crisis” due to further enrolment declines in 2025. The report is based on responses from over 150 Canadian English and French language programmes that participated in both the 2024 and 2025 surveys.
articles.insight:
Canada’s language training sector crisis may reflect broader shifts in international student preferences, potentially indicating reduced interest in Canada as a study destination due to visa processing delays, cost-of-living pressures, or evolving perceptions of post-study work opportunities—though direct spillover to other countries remains uncertain and context-dependent.  
Admissions teams should monitor application trends from key Canadian source markets (e.g., India, Nigeria, Philippines) and track whether students previously considering Canada are now applying earlier or more frequently to equivalent English-language programmes in the US, UK, Australia, or New Zealand.

articles.title: Vietnam to include artificial intelligence in school curriculum
articles.summary: Vietnam’s Ministry of Education and Training has issued a framework requiring all school students to receive 12 periods of artificial intelligence education annually. This initiative integrates AI instruction into the national school curriculum starting with the implementation of the new framework.
articles.insight:
This policy signals growing domestic investment in AI literacy across Vietnam’s education system, which may gradually elevate student expectations for advanced STEM offerings abroad—though direct impacts on enrolment demand remain uncertain without evidence of shifting preferences or capacity constraints in local higher education.  
Admissions teams should monitor Vietnamese student applications to AI- and computer science–focused programmes for early signs of increased interest, while also tracking whether local university AI curricula expansions affect enrolment patterns or scholarship-seeking behaviour over the next 2–3 intake cycles.

articles.title: UK Home Office revokes Bloomsbury Institute’s student sponsor licence
articles.summary: The UK Home Office has revoked Bloomsbury Institute’s student sponsor licence, the most serious sanction available against a licensed sponsor. This decision means the institute can no longer sponsor international students to study in the UK.
articles.insight:
This revocation signals heightened UK Home Office scrutiny of student sponsors, potentially amplifying perceptions among international applicants—especially from high-risk or overrepresented source markets—that UK visa pathways are becoming more complex or less reliable, though direct demand shifts remain unconfirmed.  
Admissions teams should monitor UK visa refusal rates, Home Office enforcement trends, and competitor messaging to assess whether this incident triggers subtle sentiment shifts in key recruitment regions or creates opportunities to position their own institutions as more stable alternatives.

articles.title: US coalition files lawsuit to challenge rule ending Duration of Status admissions for international students
articles.summary: A consortium of prominent education organizations and unions has filed a lawsuit challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s final rule that eliminates the Duration of Status (D/S) framework for international students. The coalition has submitted a complaint contesting the rule’s legality and a motion for a preliminary injunction.
articles.insight:
This rule change—though currently contested—introduces regulatory uncertainty for F-1 students in the US, potentially dampening demand from risk-averse applicants in key Asian and Latin American markets if perceived as increasing visa complexity or reducing post-study flexibility.  
Admissions teams should track litigation developments and DHS guidance closely, while reviewing messaging around US visa stability and preparing comparative talking points highlighting predictable frameworks in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.

articles.title: UK student visa applications fall again, raising fresh fears for university finances
articles.summary: UK student visa applications declined again in July. This drop has raised new concerns for universities as they enter a peak period of international recruitment.
articles.insight:
The UK’s continued decline in student visa applications may reflect shifting preferences among international students, tighter visa rules, or broader geopolitical and economic factors—but it doesn’t necessarily indicate a global demand drop, as regional dynamics and destination-specific policies vary significantly.  
Admissions teams should monitor real-time application trends from key source markets, track competitor messaging on post-study work rights and cost-of-living, and assess whether their own visa support and financial aid offerings remain competitive amid evolving student priorities.

articles.title: F-1 visa issuance drops 34% in a year as US immigration policies bite
articles.summary: The number of F-1 visas issued in the United States dropped by 34% between 2024 and 2025. Experts attribute this sharp decline to tightening US immigration policies, with an especially pronounced decrease observed among Indian students.
articles.insight:
The 34% F-1 visa drop—especially steep for Indian students—may reflect tightened US immigration enforcement and growing perceptions of reduced post-study opportunities, though it’s unclear how much this stems from policy shifts versus broader geopolitical or economic factors affecting student choice.  
Admissions teams should track real-time application and enrolment trends from India and other high-intent markets, while assessing whether competitor countries are seeing corresponding uptake—and whether institutional support services (e.g., visa guidance, career pathways) need recalibration to address evolving student risk perceptions.
